messages.content: I want to characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects remain partially identifiable in observational healthcare, even with weak instruments and bounded violations of the exclusion restriction. The work should achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over specified classes of instrument strength and exclusion violations. It should also establish sharp identification bounds and characterize when those bounds improve on bounds obtained without instruments.

There are two linked questions. The identification question is what can be learned about heterogeneous treatment effects when the instrument may be weak and its exclusion restriction may fail within stated bounds. The inference question is whether confidence sets retain at least 95% coverage uniformly across the specified strength and violation classes. Neither a narrow identified set nor good coverage alone would satisfy both parts of the goal.
What does “partially identifiable” mean here? Am I asking for a single treatment-effect value?

Not necessarily. Partial identification means the stated restrictions may leave a set or range of treatment-effect values compatible with what is observed, rather than selecting one value. For heterogeneous effects, that question concerns how effects can differ across the populations or characteristics under consideration. The goal is to characterize the remaining possibilities, not to presume that weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations still permit point identification.
Does “heterogeneous” require us to name particular patient groups now?

No particular groups are specified in the goal. Heterogeneity means the target is not merely one overall treatment effect; it concerns effects that may vary. A precise analysis would need to state which heterogeneous effects are its targets, but naming a disease, treatment, outcome, or grouping rule here would add details that have not been supplied.
How should I understand the weak-instrument part without assuming a particular measure of instrument strength?

Conceptually, a weak instrument offers limited leverage for distinguishing treatment-effect values. That makes it important not to rely on an argument that works only when the instrument is comfortably strong. The goal refers to specified classes of instrument strength, but it does not give a strength measure or a numerical cutoff. The characterization and coverage claim would have to be stated relative to whatever classes are ultimately specified.
And what does a bounded exclusion violation allow?

It allows departures from the exclusion restriction, subject to a bound, rather than treating exclusion as exact by default. The bound is part of what determines which treatment-effect values remain compatible with the restrictions. No magnitude or particular form of that bound is stated here, so the goal does not imply that any specific amount of violation is acceptable.
Is it enough to discuss weak instruments and exclusion violations separately?

The goal calls for their combined implications. Limited instrument strength can leave effects difficult to distinguish, while allowing exclusion violations can further expand what is compatible with the instrument. The question is when useful partial identification remains under the stated classes of both, not whether either issue can be handled in isolation.
What would make identification bounds “sharp”?

Sharp bounds are the tightest bounds justified by the observed information and the stated restrictions. They should not exclude a treatment-effect possibility that those restrictions actually allow, or include unnecessary slack simply because an argument was conservative. Sharpness is about faithfully describing what is identified; it does not, by itself, mean the bounds are narrow.
Then how do I compare them with bounds without instruments?

The no-instrument bounds are the comparison baseline explicitly named in the goal. The useful question is whether adding the instrument information, while allowing the specified exclusion violations, rules out any effect values that would remain possible without using instruments. To make that comparison meaningful, the two sets of bounds need to address the same effects under otherwise comparable restrictions.
Should I expect the instrument-based bounds to be strictly tighter in every case?

No such conclusion is stated. Characterizing *when* they improve includes identifying conditions under which instrument information genuinely narrows the no-instrument possibilities, as well as recognizing that weak leverage or sufficiently permissive exclusion bounds may leave no improvement. The goal calls for a characterization, not a blanket promise of strict tightening.
How does the at least 95% requirement relate to the bounds?

Identification bounds describe which effects are compatible with the population-level restrictions. Confidence sets address uncertainty from using data to learn about those effects or bounds. The requirement is that the relevant confidence-set coverage be at least 95% uniformly over the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes. Establishing sharp population bounds alone would not establish that coverage property.
What does “uniformly” add to the coverage requirement?

It rules out a claim that holds only at a convenient strength or violation level while failing elsewhere within the specified classes. In general terms, the coverage guarantee must hold across the class, including its difficult cases, rather than only at each fixed case under an argument that may break down as instrument strength changes. The exact coverage event would need to match how the target and confidence set are defined; those details are not supplied here.
So would an average of 95% coverage across the class meet the requirement?

Not on its own. An average could conceal coverage below 95% for some members of the specified classes. The stated target is at least 95% uniformly over those classes, so the guarantee cannot depend on favorable cases compensating for unfavorable ones.
Could a confidence set have the required coverage but tell us very little?

Yes. Coverage concerns how reliably the set contains its intended target; informativeness concerns how much it narrows the possibilities. A very broad set can have strong coverage without providing useful discrimination. That is why the goal separately asks for sharp identification bounds and for a characterization of when instrument-based bounds improve upon bounds without instruments.
Is there a numerical threshold here for when the instrument becomes useful, or for how large an exclusion violation can be?

The node supplies no such threshold. The only numerical requirement stated is at least 95% confidence-set coverage. Any claim about where the bounds become tighter would have to follow from the specified strength and violation classes and the resulting identification analysis, rather than from an invented cutoff.
If I put the objective in one sentence, is it fair to say that I want honest uncertainty and the tightest defensible effect bounds, while finding out whether the instrument actually adds information?

Yes, with the stated qualifications kept visible: the effects are heterogeneous, the setting is observational healthcare, instruments may be weak, and exclusion violations are bounded. “Honest uncertainty” means at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified strength and violation classes. “Tightest defensible bounds” means sharp identification bounds, and the information question is specifically when those bounds improve upon bounds obtained without instruments.

For this objective, I propose using subgroup response-type linear programs to obtain sharp bounds under bounded exclusion violations, then using exact 95% multinomial projection for inference. I would benchmark the resulting bounds against no-instrument bounds.

That is a proposed route for both parts of the objective. The subgroup response-type linear programs would address identification of heterogeneous effects under the bounded-exclusion restrictions. Exact 95% multinomial projection would address confidence-set coverage, and the no-instrument bounds would provide the benchmark for determining when the instrument narrows what remains possible.
Why use response types rather than jump straight to a treatment-effect estimate?

Response types offer a way to represent the effect possibilities that remain compatible with the observed information and the imposed restrictions. A linear program can then seek the smallest and largest value of a subgroup effect over those compatible possibilities. That fits partial identification: the proposal does not assume the information selects a single effect value.
What makes those linear-program bounds sharp, rather than merely convenient?

For a bound to be sharp, the response-type formulation must capture exactly the possibilities permitted by the stated model, including its bounded exclusion violations. Optimizing over that feasible set should give the extreme effect values that can actually be attained under those restrictions. Calling a bound sharp requires establishing that equivalence; the mere use of a linear program does not prove it.
Does introducing subgroups change the goal into a claim about particular kinds of patients?

No particular patient subgroups are specified here. The proposal uses subgroup analysis to address heterogeneous treatment effects without naming which subgroups will be studied. For each subgroup under consideration, the relevant effect and its bounds would need to be defined consistently, but no clinical grouping should be inferred from the proposal alone.
Where would the bounded exclusion violations enter the linear programs?

They would enter as restrictions on the response-type possibilities admitted by the analysis. The key is to allow the stipulated departures from exclusion while ruling out departures beyond the stipulated bounds. The proposal does not specify the mathematical form or magnitude of those bounds, so it would be premature to write down a particular constraint and present it as settled.
Could the same approach still say something if an instrument is weak?

That is what the proposed bounds would help assess. The linear programs need not assume that the instrument is strong enough for point identification: they can describe the compatible range even when instrument information offers limited leverage. Whether that range is informative, and whether it improves on the no-instrument range, remains to be characterized across the specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes.
What is meant by exact 95% multinomial projection in this proposal?

The idea is to start with a confidence region for the relevant multinomial probabilities that has at least 95% coverage under its stated conditions, then project the probabilities allowed by that region through the identification analysis. “Exact” distinguishes the proposed coverage basis from relying solely on an approximation that might be unreliable in difficult cases. The proposal does not specify a particular multinomial-region construction.
Does projecting an exact multinomial region automatically give an exact 95% confidence set for every heterogeneous effect?

The coverage argument needs to be made for the stated target. If the true multinomial probabilities are in a region with at least 95% coverage, and the projection includes every target value compatible with probabilities in that region under the maintained restrictions, that inclusion can support at least 95% coverage for the appropriate partially identified target. It does not by itself establish that every possible way of defining or reporting subgroup effect sets has the desired guarantee.
I also need uniform coverage, not just a nominal 95% at one setting. How should the proposal be read on that point?

The proposed exact projection is intended to support the goal of at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the specified classes of instrument strength and exclusion violations. To establish that claim, the multinomial coverage argument and the projection argument must apply throughout those classes, including weak-instrument cases. The word “exact” is not a substitute for demonstrating the uniform guarantee.
Would separate 95% calculations for each subgroup necessarily give the required guarantee if I discuss them together?

Not necessarily. Coverage for each separately reported subgroup target is different from simultaneous coverage for several subgroup targets. The inferential target and coverage event would need to be stated before claiming a joint guarantee. The proposal specifies exact 95% multinomial projection, but it does not specify whether the intended coverage statement is separate or simultaneous across subgroups.
How should I set up the benchmark against no-instrument bounds without prejudging the outcome?

Compare bounds for the same subgroup effect under the relevant restrictions, once using the permitted instrument information and once using the no-instrument benchmark. Then ask whether the instrument-based sharp bounds exclude possibilities that the no-instrument bounds retain. The proposal calls for that benchmark; it does not claim in advance that the instrument will tighten the bounds in every subgroup or throughout every allowed strength and violation class.
So improvement is about identification, while the exact projection is about inference?

Primarily, yes. The sharp linear-program bounds and their comparison with no-instrument bounds concern what the restrictions identify. Exact 95% multinomial projection concerns uncertainty in learning from observed data. Keeping those questions distinct matters: an instrument could improve population identification without every resulting confidence set being narrow, and a well-covered confidence set would not by itself establish an identification improvement.
What would this proposed approach let us conclude right now?

At this stage it specifies a method to investigate the goal, not a completed result. It proposes subgroup response-type linear programs for sharp bounded-exclusion bounds, exact 95% multinomial projection for inference, and comparison with no-instrument bounds. Sharpness, uniform coverage over the specified classes, and the conditions under which the instrument improves the bounds would still need to be established.
The next question is: which subgroup first-stage strengths and exclusion budgets yield response-type bounds strictly narrower than no-instrument Manski bounds?

That asks for a subgroup-specific characterization of when the instrument adds identifying information. For each subgroup, compare the response-type bounds obtained at a stated first-stage strength and exclusion budget with the no-instrument Manski bounds for the same effect. Strict narrowing means the instrument-based interval rules out at least some values retained by that benchmark; it should not be inferred merely from having introduced an instrument.
Can we say that any nonzero subgroup first stage is enough?

Not from the question alone. A nonzero first stage may provide some leverage, but an allowed exclusion violation may offset or limit what that leverage tells us about the effect. Whether the response-type bounds are strictly narrower depends on the combination of subgroup first-stage strength, the exclusion budget, and the other restrictions defining those bounds. No universal numerical cutoff has been supplied.
Would it be fair to look for a threshold in the exclusion budget at each subgroup first-stage strength?

That is one way to formulate the question, provided such a threshold is actually justified by the bound construction. You could ask, for a given subgroup and first-stage strength, which permitted exclusion budgets still produce a strict improvement over the Manski bounds. The question itself does not establish that there is a single threshold, what its value is, or that it has the same form across subgroups.
Why emphasize subgroup first-stage strength instead of just instrument strength overall?

Because the question concerns heterogeneous effects and asks specifically which *subgroup* first-stage strengths matter. An overall measure might not describe the leverage relevant to a particular subgroup's effect. The comparison should therefore be made for each subgroup effect using the strength information pertinent to that subgroup, without presuming that every subgroup has the same improvement.
How should I interpret the exclusion budget in this comparison?

It is the amount of exclusion-restriction departure permitted in the response-type analysis. The comparison asks whether the instrument remains informative after allowing departures within that budget. The question specifies neither units nor a particular way to encode the budget, so a numerical characterization would require a definition before it could be stated accurately.
If the instrument-based interval has the same lower bound as the Manski interval but a higher upper bound, is that an improvement?

No. A higher upper bound would not narrow the interval at that end. For strict narrowing relative to the no-instrument Manski interval, the instrument-based bound must eliminate at least some values in the Manski interval while remaining a valid comparison for the same target. This might appear as a higher lower endpoint, a lower upper endpoint, or both; merely changing an endpoint is not enough if it expands the allowed range.
Do both endpoints have to move inward?

Not necessarily. If the response-type interval is contained in the no-instrument Manski interval and at least one endpoint moves inward, it is strictly narrower as a set. If instead you mean a smaller numerical width without containment, that is a different comparison. Stating which sense of “strictly narrower” is intended would make the answer to the question unambiguous.
Could the bounds be sharp yet fail to beat the Manski bounds?

Yes. Sharpness means the response-type bounds describe the full range allowed by their stated restrictions, without avoidable slack. It does not guarantee that those restrictions exclude values allowed by the no-instrument Manski benchmark. Determining when there is strict narrowing is a separate question.
Should the response-type bounds be compared with Manski bounds calculated for each subgroup, rather than with a pooled no-instrument bound?

To answer this subgroup-specific question directly, the benchmark should address the same subgroup effect as the response-type bounds. Otherwise a difference in intervals could reflect a change in the target, not information supplied by the instrument. Nothing here specifies how subgroup effects are defined, so the comparison must keep their definitions aligned once specified.
Is the answer necessarily a simple rule like “stronger first stage and smaller exclusion budget”?

That phrase expresses a useful intuition, but it is not yet the requested characterization. A larger permitted exclusion violation can make more effect values admissible, and instrument leverage can depend on subgroup strength, but the actual strict-narrowing condition must follow from the response-type bounds and the Manski benchmark. A simple rule should not be asserted without showing that it holds under the specified restrictions.
Can you be more precise about what would count as answering “which” combinations work, without inventing values?

An answer would specify, for each subgroup, the combinations of first-stage strength and exclusion budget for which the sharp response-type identified interval is a proper subset of the corresponding no-instrument Manski interval. It would also identify combinations for which the comparison does not show strict narrowing, if those occur. That describes the desired characterization without pretending that a numerical region or boundary has already been established.
What if the comparison changes across subgroups?

Then the characterization should report that subgroup dependence rather than replace it with one universal claim. One subgroup's first-stage strength and permitted exclusion budget could yield a different comparison from another's. The present question asks which combinations work; it does not say that the answer must be identical across subgroups.
Does asking about first-stage strengths and exclusion budgets by itself tell us that a strict improvement exists anywhere?

No. It poses the issue to determine. The response-type and Manski bounds have to be defined and compared before concluding whether any particular combination produces strict narrowing. If no combination in a specified class does, that would be part of an eventual answer, not a premise of this question.

Here is a specific hypothesis addressing the subgroup-bound comparison: in HealthSim-1, a first-stage strength of at least 0.20 and an exclusion-risk budget of at most 0.02 yield subgroup LP bounds at least 10% narrower than no-instrument bounds.

That is a hypothesis about HealthSim-1, not an established result. It combines two conditions—first-stage strength ≥0.20 and exclusion-risk budget ≤0.02—and predicts a quantitative improvement: subgroup linear-program bounds at least 10% narrower than the corresponding no-instrument bounds.
Are both numerical conditions meant to apply together?

Yes. The stated prediction is for the combination of first-stage strength ≥0.20 *and* exclusion-risk budget ≤0.02. It does not separately claim that either condition alone is sufficient for at least 10% narrowing.
Do the thresholds include their endpoints?

They do as written. “At least 0.20” includes a first-stage strength equal to 0.20, and “at most 0.02” includes an exclusion-risk budget equal to 0.02. The proposed improvement is likewise inclusive: narrowing of exactly 10% would meet the stated threshold.
What does “at least 10% narrower” compare?

It compares the subgroup LP bounds with no-instrument bounds for the same subgroup effect in HealthSim-1. If “narrower” is measured by interval width, the claim would mean the LP interval has no more than 90% of the width of its no-instrument counterpart. That is a way to interpret the percentage, not a report that the comparison has already been calculated.
Should I call the no-instrument comparison the Manski bounds?

The motivating question calls them no-instrument Manski bounds. For this hypothesis, the essential point is that the benchmark is the corresponding no-instrument bound for the same subgroup effect. Using the Manski label is appropriate if that is the no-instrument construction being compared; the hypothesis does not add a separate benchmark.
Does 10% narrowing mean each endpoint moves inward by 10%?

No. A percentage reduction in the width of a bound does not specify how much either endpoint moves. One endpoint might account for the narrowing, or both might contribute. The hypothesis states a bound-width improvement, without making an endpoint-by-endpoint prediction.
Could I treat the first-stage value of 0.20 as a universal cutoff?

No. The numerical hypothesis is explicitly situated in HealthSim-1. It does not claim that 0.20 is a universal first-stage cutoff in observational healthcare, or that the same improvement follows in every setting.
Is the exclusion-risk budget of 0.02 a claim about the actual size of any violation?

Not as stated. It is the permitted exclusion-risk budget in the hypothesis. The statement predicts what the subgroup LP bounds would do when that budget is at most 0.02, alongside first-stage strength of at least 0.20. It does not report a measured violation or specify further units for the budget.
Does the hypothesis tell us what happens if the first stage is below 0.20 or the budget is above 0.02?
No. Those combinations fall outside the conditions named in the hypothesis. The statement does not predict that their bounds fail to improve; it simply makes no at-least-10% claim for them.
Would any strict narrowing confirm this particular hypothesis?

Not necessarily. Strict narrowing could be less than 10%. This hypothesis predicts at least a 10% reduction in subgroup LP bound width, relative to no-instrument bounds, under the stated HealthSim-1 conditions. A smaller reduction would address the broader question of whether instruments help but would not meet this numerical prediction.
Am I also claiming that every subgroup must show the same amount of narrowing?

The hypothesis says “subgroup LP bounds” but does not spell out whether the ≥10% requirement applies to every subgroup considered or to a particular set of subgroup comparisons. That scope would need to be specified to assess it unambiguously. It should not be silently strengthened into a claim about every conceivable subgroup.
Does this hypothesis establish sharpness or 95% confidence-set coverage?

No. It predicts a particular identification-bound improvement under stated conditions in HealthSim-1. Sharpness of the LP bounds and at least 95% confidence-set coverage are distinct properties to establish; neither follows just from the ≥10% width hypothesis.
So the careful wording is that this is a proposed quantitative answer to when the subgroup bounds improve, rather than an observed HealthSim-1 result?

Exactly. The proposed answer is conditional: in HealthSim-1, first-stage strength ≥0.20 together with exclusion-risk budget ≤0.02 is hypothesized to yield subgroup LP bounds ≥10% narrower than corresponding no-instrument bounds. The numerical improvement remains a hypothesis, not a completed comparison or a general guarantee.
To evaluate the HealthSim-1 hypothesis, simulate across first-stage strengths from 0 to 0.30 and exclusion budgets from 0 to 0.05, then compare subgroup LP bound widths against Manski bounds.

That activity examines the bound-width comparison across both dimensions, rather than only at the hypothesized conditions. For each subgroup comparison in HealthSim-1, the question is how wide the LP bounds are relative to the corresponding no-instrument Manski bounds. The stated ranges include first-stage strengths of 0–0.30 and exclusion budgets of 0–0.05; no simulation results are supplied yet.
How does this evaluate the numerical hypothesis?

The hypothesis predicts at least 10% narrower subgroup LP bounds when first-stage strength is at least 0.20 and the exclusion-risk budget is at most 0.02. Those values lie within the proposed simulation ranges. Comparing widths under those conditions with the corresponding Manski widths would address that prediction, while the wider ranges allow the comparison to be examined beyond those conditions without presuming its outcome.
Why include first-stage strengths below 0.20?

They are part of the stated 0–0.30 range and help characterize how the LP-versus-Manski width comparison varies with first-stage strength. The hypothesis makes no at-least-10% prediction below 0.20, so observing or calculating a comparison there would not, by itself, test that particular conditional claim.
And why include exclusion budgets above 0.02?

The activity specifies budgets through 0.05, which extends beyond the hypothesis’s ≤0.02 condition. Those comparisons can help describe what happens as more exclusion risk is permitted. They should not be treated as covered by the hypothesis’s ≥10% narrowing prediction.
Does the first-stage range include zero?
Yes. The stated range is 0–0.30, so it includes 0. Likewise, the exclusion-budget range of 0–0.05 includes 0. The activity does not specify what the resulting widths will be at either endpoint.
What exactly should be held comparable when we look at the two widths?

Each LP width should be compared with the Manski-bound width for the same subgroup effect. Otherwise, a difference in width might reflect different targets rather than the contribution of the instrument under the permitted exclusion budget. The activity specifies the comparison, but not particular subgroup definitions or numerical widths.
Is “narrower” about interval width here, rather than whether each endpoint moves inward?

Yes. This activity explicitly compares subgroup LP *widths* against Manski bounds. A width comparison measures the span of each bound; it does not, on its own, say which endpoint moves or establish that one interval is contained in the other.
Can we express the hypothesized 10% improvement directly in terms of widths?

Where the Manski width is positive, an LP width no greater than 90% of that Manski width expresses “at least 10% narrower.” That provides a clear way to read the numerical hypothesis for a comparable subgroup effect. If a percentage comparison is not defined for a particular benchmark width, that case would need to be handled explicitly rather than assigned an invented percentage.
Should I read the 0–0.30 and 0–0.05 ranges as already showing where improvement occurs?

No. They describe the HealthSim-1 simulation activity’s first-stage and exclusion-budget ranges. They are not findings about which combinations narrow the bounds. The width comparisons are what would answer that question.
Does simulating over these ranges itself prove that the subgroup LP bounds are sharp?

No. The activity compares calculated LP widths with Manski widths. Sharpness is a separate claim about whether the response-type linear programs attain the tightest bounds implied by their stated restrictions. A width comparison cannot establish sharpness merely because it spans the specified ranges.
Would this activity establish the goal’s uniform at least 95% confidence-set coverage?

Not by itself. The specified activity is a simulation of HealthSim-1 across first-stage strengths and exclusion budgets, with subgroup LP widths compared against Manski bounds. That addresses the identification-bound comparison. It does not state a confidence-set coverage evaluation or establish uniform at least 95% coverage.
If a width is smaller outside the hypothesis’s thresholds, how should I interpret that?

It would speak to the broader question of when LP bounds are narrower than Manski bounds, if such a result were obtained. It would not change what the HealthSim-1 hypothesis actually predicts: at least 10% narrowing under first-stage strength ≥0.20 together with exclusion-risk budget ≤0.02. The activity does not yet report any such result inside or outside that region.
What about a comparison exactly at first-stage 0.20 and exclusion budget 0.02?

Both equalities satisfy the hypothesis’s inclusive conditions, and both values fall within the activity’s stated ranges. A HealthSim-1 width comparison at that combination would therefore bear directly on the ≥10% narrowing prediction for the relevant subgroup effect, without implying anything about the outcome in advance.
So the task for this activity is to examine the subgroup width comparisons throughout the specified ranges, with particular attention to the hypothesized combination?

Yes. In HealthSim-1, the activity is to simulate first-stage strengths from 0 to 0.30 and exclusion budgets from 0 to 0.05 and compare subgroup LP bound widths with corresponding no-instrument Manski bounds. The ≥0.20 and ≤0.02 conditions identify the part of that range relevant to the proposed ≥10% narrowing hypothesis; the comparison has not yet been reported.
On HealthSim-1, the subgroup LP bounds were at least 12% narrower than the Manski bounds when first-stage strength was at least 0.20 and the exclusion budget was at most 0.02.

That is a reported bound-width result for HealthSim-1. Under the joint conditions first-stage strength ≥0.20 and exclusion budget ≤0.02, the subgroup LP bounds were at least 12% narrower than the corresponding no-instrument Manski bounds. It is a result about those bounds under those conditions, not a universal claim about other settings.
Does “at least 12%” mean the reduction was exactly 12%?

No. It gives a minimum reported reduction. A comparison showing exactly 12% narrowing would satisfy the statement, as would a larger reduction; the statement does not provide the individual percentages.
Can you express that as a width comparison?

Where the corresponding Manski width is positive, at least 12% narrowing means the subgroup LP width is no more than 88% of that Manski width. That describes the relative widths without specifying either bound’s numerical endpoints.
Do the first-stage and exclusion-budget conditions have to hold at the same time?
Yes. The reported result is conditional on first-stage strength being ≥0.20 and exclusion budget being ≤0.02 together. It does not say that either condition alone yields at least 12% narrowing.
Are comparisons at exactly 0.20 and exactly 0.02 included?
Yes. Both inequalities are inclusive: a first-stage strength of 0.20 meets ≥0.20, and an exclusion budget of 0.02 meets ≤0.02.
What does this tell us about the value of using the instrument in HealthSim-1?

For the reported subgroup comparisons under those joint conditions, the instrument-based LP bounds have smaller widths than the no-instrument Manski bounds. That is evidence of a quantitative improvement in the bound-width comparison in HealthSim-1. It does not specify how much either endpoint changes.
Could a smaller width alone tell me that the LP interval is contained inside the Manski interval?

Not by itself. An interval can be shorter without being contained in another interval. The reported evidence compares widths; establishing containment or identifying which effect values are excluded would require endpoint information that is not stated here.
Does the result say anything about first-stage strengths below 0.20?
It makes no at-least-12% claim for strengths below 0.20. It also does not say that subgroup LP bounds fail to narrow there; that would require a separate comparison.
And if the exclusion budget is above 0.02?
The reported condition no longer applies. The statement does not give a width reduction, or say whether one exists, for budgets above 0.02.
Can I generalize this percentage to observational healthcare settings outside HealthSim-1?

No. The at-least-12% figure is reported for HealthSim-1 under the stated first-stage and exclusion-budget conditions. Applying that percentage elsewhere would require additional evidence; it is not implied by this result.
Does this width result establish that the LP bounds are sharp?

No. A 12% or greater width reduction is a comparison with Manski bounds. Sharpness asks whether the LP bounds are the tightest bounds permitted by the stated response-type and exclusion restrictions. The reported width comparison does not establish that property on its own.
What about the requirement for at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes?

This evidence reports subgroup identification-bound widths, not confidence-set coverage. It therefore does not establish an at-least-95% uniform coverage guarantee, even though that remains a separate requirement of the broader objective.
So the precise takeaway is limited to the HealthSim-1 width comparison?

Yes: for first-stage strength ≥0.20 and exclusion budget ≤0.02 in HealthSim-1, the reported subgroup LP bounds were at least 12% narrower in width than the corresponding no-instrument Manski bounds. The statement does not supply endpoint comparisons, results outside those conditions, or an inference-coverage finding.
Let’s retain the full weak-instrument grid for coverage testing, but prioritize first-stage strengths of at least 0.20 when focusing on the simulated width gains of at least 12%.

That separates two purposes. Coverage testing will retain the full weak-instrument grid, including its weaker first-stage settings. Prioritizing first stages ≥0.20 concerns where to focus attention on the ≥12% simulated width gains; it does not narrow the coverage-testing grid.
Does prioritizing ≥0.20 mean we can leave weaker first stages out of the coverage assessment?

No. Retaining the full weak-instrument grid is an explicit part of the decision. The priority for ≥0.20 is about the simulated bound-width gains, not permission to omit weaker settings from coverage testing.
Why keep the weak settings if the width-gain priority is elsewhere?

Width improvement and coverage answer different questions. A setting need not be the focus of the ≥12% simulated width-gain discussion to matter for assessing coverage under weak instruments. Testing coverage only where bounds look especially informative would not address performance across the full grid you chose to retain.
Is ≥0.20 now the minimum first-stage strength for the method?

No. It is a prioritization threshold for examining the simulated width gains. The decision does not impose ≥0.20 as a general requirement for applying the method, nor does it remove lower first-stage strengths from coverage testing.
Should I describe the ≥12% gain as a guaranteed improvement whenever the first stage reaches 0.20?

No. The decision refers to ≥12% *simulated* width gains and prioritizes ≥0.20 first stages in that context. It does not turn the observed simulation comparison into a guarantee for every setting or every other combination of conditions.
Does the priority change the comparison with the no-instrument bounds?

No. The width-gain priority still concerns the comparison of subgroup LP bound widths with the corresponding no-instrument bounds. It changes where attention is concentrated in discussing those simulated gains, not what serves as the comparison benchmark.
Could we say that coverage has already been shown on the full grid because we decided to retain it?

No. Retaining the grid specifies the scope for coverage testing; it is not a coverage result. The at-least-95% uniform coverage goal would still require an appropriate assessment or argument across its specified classes.
How do I keep the two emphases clear in a write-up?

State them separately: retain the full weak-instrument grid for coverage testing, and prioritize first-stage strengths ≥0.20 when examining the ≥12% simulated width gains. That wording keeps the broader coverage-testing scope distinct from the narrower emphasis on bound-width improvement.
Does prioritizing those first stages say that lower first stages cannot yield narrower bounds?

No. A priority is not a negative finding about the rest of the grid. This decision does not establish whether lower first-stage strengths do or do not yield narrower bounds; it simply keeps them within coverage testing while directing attention to ≥0.20 for the stated simulated gains.
And the ≥12% figure remains a simulated width result, not a confidence-coverage percentage?

Correct. The ≥12% figure concerns simulated bound-width gains. It should not be confused with the separate objective of at least 95% confidence-set coverage. The decision preserves the full weak-instrument grid for testing that coverage objective.

For the next stage, I plan to prove that the subgroup LP bounds are sharp and validate uniform 95% exact-projection coverage across first-stage strengths from 0 to 0.30 and exclusion budgets from 0 to 0.05. I’ll prioritize Manski-bound comparisons at first-stage strengths of at least 0.20.

That plan has three distinct parts: establish sharpness of the LP identification bounds, validate the uniform 95% coverage claim for exact projection across the full stated ranges, and give priority to comparisons with no-instrument Manski bounds at first-stage strengths ≥0.20. The priority for comparisons does not reduce the 0–0.30 first-stage or 0–0.05 exclusion-budget coverage scope.
What would proving LP sharpness require, in general terms?

It would require showing that the LP feasible set accurately represents the possibilities allowed by the stated response-type and bounded-exclusion restrictions, and that the LP extrema are attainable within those restrictions. That is what makes the resulting endpoints the tightest justified identification bounds, rather than just bounds produced by an optimization routine. This is work the plan calls for, not a proof already in hand.

I propose constructing sensitivity polytopes that account for both exclusion violations and IV confounding. We would project exact multinomial regions onto sharp subgroup treatment-effect bounds, then compare their widths with no-instrument Manski bounds when instruments are weak.

That proposal treats exclusion violations and IV confounding as two distinct sensitivity dimensions. The polytopes would represent effect possibilities allowed under their specified restrictions; projection of exact multinomial regions would address uncertainty in the observed probabilities. The identification bounds would then be compared with Manski bounds for the same subgroup effects under weak instruments. Sharpness, coverage, and any width improvement remain properties to establish, not outcomes asserted by the proposal.
What does adding IV confounding mean conceptually? Is it just another name for exclusion violation?

No. An exclusion violation concerns whether the instrument can affect the outcome through a route other than the treatment. IV confounding concerns whether the instrument is associated with factors relevant to the outcome in a way that challenges its validity as an instrument. The proposal allows sensitivity to both issues; specifying a restriction on one does not automatically restrict the other.
Does the proposal say that IV confounding definitely exists in the healthcare setting?

No. It proposes a sensitivity analysis that accommodates possible IV confounding alongside exclusion violations. That is different from reporting that either violation has been observed, measuring its magnitude, or assigning it a cause.
Why call the sensitivity sets polytopes?

A polytope is a feasible set described by linear constraints. In the proposed approach, it would organize the combinations of underlying probabilities or response-type possibilities permitted by the observed information and the chosen sensitivity restrictions. Calling a set a polytope requires that its actual formulation have that structure; the proposal does not provide its constraints or numerical sensitivity limits.
Do I need separate sensitivity allowances for exclusion and IV confounding?

The two departures need to be represented distinctly enough that the permissible combinations are clear. The proposal does not specify whether their limits are expressed as separate budgets, coupled restrictions, or some other polytope constraints. Assigning particular allowances now would add details not stated in the proposal.
What is being projected from the multinomial region?

The multinomial region represents uncertainty about the relevant observed cell probabilities. Projection carries the probabilities admitted by that region through the sensitivity polytope and the subgroup-effect calculation, retaining effect values compatible with some permitted probabilities and restrictions. The proposal does not specify the cells, a particular region construction, or the resulting confidence-set endpoints.
If the multinomial region is exact, does that automatically make the projected effect set exactly 95%?

Not automatically. The region’s coverage level and the projection’s inclusion argument must be specified for the intended target. An exact region with a suitable coverage guarantee can support a projected confidence set with at least that coverage under its maintained restrictions, but projection may be conservative. The proposal itself does not state an achieved coverage rate; the broader goal calls for at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified classes.
What is the difference between the sharp subgroup bounds and the projected confidence sets?

Sharp subgroup bounds describe the range of effects compatible with population-level information and the stated sensitivity restrictions. Projected confidence sets also account for uncertainty in estimating the observed multinomial probabilities. A sharp population bound need not be narrow, and a projection with sound coverage does not by itself prove that the underlying identification bounds are sharp.
Can a polytope be used to obtain sharp effect bounds merely by optimizing over it?

Optimization yields extrema for the polytope as formulated. To call those bounds sharp for the proposed model, one must additionally show that the polytope captures exactly its admissible possibilities and that its extrema are attainable. If the formulation leaves out valid possibilities or includes unnecessary restrictions, the optimization result alone cannot establish the desired sharpness.
How do weak instruments affect this sensitivity analysis?

Weak instruments can provide limited information for separating treatment effects from the other possibilities allowed by the sensitivity restrictions. The proposed projection and width comparisons therefore have to remain meaningful without assuming a strong first stage. Weakness does not by itself determine whether the sharp bounds improve on Manski bounds or whether the projected confidence sets attain their intended coverage.
Does the proposal set a cutoff for what counts as weak?

No. It names weak instruments as a condition of interest but supplies no first-stage threshold, sensitivity-budget magnitude, or range of instrument strengths. Any quantitative cutoff would have to be specified separately rather than inferred from this proposal.
Could allowing IV confounding and exclusion violations both at once make the identified bounds wider?

Conceptually, allowing more possibilities can weaken identification, depending on how the sensitivity restrictions are defined. But the proposal provides no particular polytope or computed bounds, so it does not state a numerical width change or guarantee that every subgroup responds the same way.
Does the no-instrument Manski benchmark also include those sensitivity assumptions?

A meaningful comparison must define the no-instrument benchmark and keep the subgroup-effect target and other relevant restrictions aligned. Then one can ask what, if anything, the instrument contributes under the permitted exclusion and IV-confounding sensitivity. The proposal identifies Manski bounds as the no-instrument width benchmark, but does not spell out the full restriction set for either side.
If the projected confidence set is narrower than a Manski interval, have we demonstrated that the instrument tightens identification?

Not on that comparison alone. A projected confidence set is an inferential object; a Manski identification bound is a population identification object. To assess whether the instrument tightens identification, compare the sharp subgroup identification bounds with the corresponding no-instrument Manski bounds. Coverage and the width of projected confidence sets should be evaluated separately.
And if the instrument-based identification interval has smaller width, is that necessarily strict set containment?

No. A shorter interval need not lie wholly inside another interval. The proposal explicitly calls for a width comparison, so that can characterize width gains. If the desired conclusion is that the instrument rules out particular values allowed by the Manski interval, the relevant endpoints or set relationship must also be checked.
Does an exact multinomial region necessarily give simultaneous coverage for every subgroup effect?

That depends on the region’s coverage event and how it is projected onto the collection of subgroup effects. A joint region can provide a basis for simultaneous inference if the construction and inclusion argument cover all the intended targets together. The proposal does not specify whether its coverage claim is joint across subgroups or separate for each, so simultaneity should not be assumed merely from the word “exact.”
What would a uniform 95% claim have to account for under this proposal?

It would have to state the instrument-strength class and the allowed combinations of exclusion violations and IV confounding, then justify at least 95% confidence-set coverage throughout that class for the defined subgroup targets. A favorable calculation at selected settings would not, on its own, establish uniform coverage. Neither the classes nor a coverage result are supplied in this proposal.
Is it possible to have valid coverage while the instrument contributes no width gain over Manski?

Yes, conceptually. Coverage concerns whether the projected sets reliably contain their intended targets; a Manski-relative gain concerns whether the instrument-based identification bounds narrow the no-instrument possibilities. The proposal investigates both, and it does not require a width gain at every weak-instrument setting as a precondition for coverage.
Can you state what this proposal actually commits us to examining, without claiming that it already works?

Construct sensitivity polytopes for exclusion violations and IV confounding; project exact multinomial regions onto subgroup treatment effects to pursue inference for sharp identification bounds; and, under weak instruments, compare the subgroup bound widths with corresponding no-instrument Manski widths. Whether the resulting bounds are sharp, the confidence sets have the required coverage, and the instrument improves the benchmark remains to be established.
At first-stage strength 0.03, how much instrument–outcome confounding can the sensitivity polytopes tolerate before the subgroup bounds lose their width advantage over no-instrument Manski bounds?

Is the first-stage value of 0.03 a threshold for acceptable confounding?

What counts as losing the Manski-width advantage?

If the advantage means a strictly smaller subgroup bound width, it is lost when that strict width reduction no longer holds. Equal widths would mean no remaining width advantage; a wider subgroup bound would not have one either. This is a comparison of bounds for the same subgroup effect, not a comparison of coverage percentages.
Would every subgroup necessarily lose its advantage at the same confounding allowance?

No common limit is specified. The sensitivity-polytope bounds and the Manski benchmark concern subgroup effects, so any confounding limit would have to be characterized for the subgroups under consideration. The question leaves open whether the limits differ or whether some subgroup has no initial width advantage under the specified restrictions.
Do we already know there is a single cutoff where the advantage disappears?

No. A single cutoff would require suitable structure in how the admissible sensitivity polytopes change as confounding is permitted to increase, and in how the bound widths respond. The question asks how much can be tolerated; it does not establish monotonicity, a unique cutoff, or even a particular parameterization of confounding.
Could you explain what a threshold-style answer would look like without assigning a number?

One possible form would identify, for each subgroup, the confounding allowances at first-stage 0.03 for which the sharp sensitivity-polytope bound is strictly narrower in width than its no-instrument Manski bound, and those for which it is not. If those allowances form a region with a meaningful boundary, that boundary could be reported. Whether they actually have that form must be established rather than presumed.
How should exclusion violations be handled while we ask about instrument–outcome confounding?

They should remain explicitly represented in the sensitivity restrictions. To isolate how the width comparison changes with the permitted instrument–outcome confounding, the relevant exclusion-violation conditions must be stated and kept comparable across the comparisons. The question gives no particular exclusion budget or joint restriction for the two sensitivity dimensions.
Is instrument–outcome confounding interchangeable with an exclusion violation in that calculation?

No. They are distinct departures that the proposed polytopes are intended to accommodate. A limit on exclusion violations does not, without further restrictions, give a numerical limit on instrument–outcome confounding. Combining them without specifying how each enters the polytope would make the requested confounding tolerance ambiguous.
Why compare to Manski bounds instead of just asking whether the subgroup bound is narrow?

The Manski bounds provide the specified no-instrument benchmark. A subgroup bound can appear narrow or wide in isolation, but the question is whether the instrument still contributes a width advantage once instrument–outcome confounding is allowed. That requires a like-for-like comparison with the no-instrument bound for the same subgroup effect.
If the sensitivity-polytope bound becomes wider, does that alone mean the instrument has lost its advantage?

Not necessarily. Its width could increase while remaining smaller than the corresponding Manski width. The advantage is lost only according to the comparison with that benchmark, not merely because the bound changes as the confounding allowance changes.
Can I use confidence-set width in place of the sharp subgroup bound width for this question?

Not without changing the question. It asks when *subgroup bounds* lose their Manski-width advantage, an identification comparison. A projected confidence set additionally reflects uncertainty in the observed probabilities. Its width and coverage are important but do not by themselves determine whether the sharp identification bounds outperform Manski bounds.
Does finding a positive width advantage at one confounding allowance tell us coverage is at least 95%?

No. Width advantage and confidence-set coverage are separate properties. A confounding allowance could yield bounds narrower than Manski bounds without the projected confidence sets meeting their intended coverage, or coverage could hold where there is no width advantage. This question specifically seeks the confounding limit for the bound-width comparison at first-stage 0.03.
Would the width comparison be meaningful if the sensitivity-polytope bounds were not sharp?

You could compare calculated widths, but a claim about the sharp subgroup identification bounds requires showing that the polytope represents the admissible possibilities and that its extrema are attainable. Otherwise, an apparent advantage might reflect how a non-sharp bound was constructed rather than the identifying information available under the specified restrictions.
Is the answer necessarily a universal amount of confounding for observational healthcare?

No. The question is tied to first-stage strength 0.03, specified subgroup effects, sensitivity polytopes, and corresponding Manski bounds. It supplies neither a universal confounding measure nor a universal limit. Any eventual answer should be confined to the restrictions and subgroups for which the comparison is actually established.

It should define the permitted instrument–outcome confounding within the exclusion-and-IV-confounding sensitivity polytopes, obtain the sharp subgroup bounds at first-stage 0.03, and compare each bound’s width with its no-instrument Manski benchmark as the confounding allowance varies. Would a 2% gain mean the instrument has lost its width advantage altogether?

Should the Manski bound be calculated for the same subgroup treatment effect?

Yes. Each sensitivity-polytope subgroup bound must be compared with the no-instrument Manski bound for the same subgroup effect. Otherwise, the relative width could reflect a difference in targets rather than the instrument’s contribution under the permitted confounding and exclusion violations.
Is the predicted 3% reduction a claim about projected confidence-set widths?

No. It concerns the width of subgroup identification bounds relative to Manski bounds. The hypothesis does not give a numerical prediction about projected confidence-set width or about confidence-set coverage.

Am I claiming the gain for every conceivable subgroup and every possible budget assignment below those limits?

The hypothesis does not identify particular subgroups or specify the quantifier over possible subgroup-budget assignments. Those details would have to be defined to test the prediction unambiguously. Would a sharpness proof at one first-stage strength prove the result across the grids?

How should I understand ‘uniform ≥95% projection coverage across weak-IV grids’?

Is getting an overall average coverage of 95% enough?

No. An overall average could conceal a setting with coverage below 95%. Uniform coverage requires the guarantee to apply across the settings in its stated scope; favorable settings cannot compensate for an unfavorable one.
If simulations at every grid cell report at least 95%, can I call the uniform result proved?

Those simulations would be evidence about the examined cells, but empirical coverage estimates have sampling uncertainty. Does projection itself ensure coverage when the instrument is very weak?

Projection can be part of a coverage argument, but its validity depends on the coverage of the underlying multinomial region, the restrictions used in projecting it, and the target to be covered. Should the coverage claim be simultaneous across subgroups?

Do the Manski gains refer to confidence-set widths or to the sharp identification bounds?

Why insist on a comparable Manski-based benchmark?

A width difference is interpretable only if both sets concern the same subgroup effect and use a clearly defined comparison. If a subgroup with n≥400 has sharp bounds and adequate coverage, must it also have a ≥3% gain?

Not by itself. It names the range for the planned gain validation. An assertion that 400 is an exact cutoff would require comparisons establishing what happens at relevant sizes below and above it under clearly defined conditions. The plan does not make that cutoff claim.
Should we assume the ≥3% gain persists at every permitted confounding level or first-stage strength?

No. The plan calls for validation, not an advance guarantee across all sensitivity and strength settings. The scope of any eventual gain claim must identify the subgroup effects, weak-IV settings, and confounding and exclusion restrictions actually covered.

It would meet a properly defined ≥3% width-gain criterion, but width alone would not establish set containment. If the intended conclusion is that particular treatment-effect values permitted by the Manski bound have been ruled out, the endpoints or full set relationship must also be examined.

Not yet. The plan is not a completed proof or a general result for all observational healthcare settings.

I propose calibrating subgroup exclusion budgets using negative-control outcomes and capped bias ratios, then projecting joint 95% multinomial regions through sharp response-type LPs.

That proposal has a calibration component and an inference component. Negative-control outcomes and capped bias ratios would inform the subgroup-specific limits on exclusion violations. The joint 95% multinomial regions would then be projected through response-type LPs to obtain confidence sets for the subgroup effects. The proposal does not yet specify the controls, the caps, the resulting budgets, or a coverage result for the projected sets.
What would a negative-control outcome contribute to setting an exclusion budget?

It could provide information relevant to how large an exclusion departure it is reasonable to allow, provided the negative-control outcome has a justified relationship to the violation of interest. That relationship needs to be stated: an association involving a negative control does not automatically equal the exclusion violation for a treatment outcome. Here, using negative-control outcomes for calibration is the proposal, not a completed measurement.
Does this mean we already know which negative-control outcomes to use?

No. None are named. The proposal also does not state their observed associations or the assumptions that would link those associations to exclusion violations in particular subgroups. Choosing a control merely because it is available would not, by itself, justify a calibrated budget.
Why make the exclusion budgets subgroup-specific?

The restrictions would then express the permitted exclusion departure for each subgroup effect under consideration, instead of requiring a single unspecified allowance to describe all subgroups. Calibration would have to respect the evidence and assumptions applicable to each subgroup. The proposal does not say whether the resulting budget values would differ.
What is a capped bias ratio supposed to do?

Conceptually, a bias ratio would relate the negative-control information to the exclusion departure allowed in the analysis, while a cap would limit how large that ratio may be under the sensitivity specification. The actual definition of the ratio, its cap, and the way they translate into a subgroup exclusion budget are not given. The cap is a restriction to justify, not evidence that the true ratio lies below it.
Can we infer a particular numerical cap from the phrase ‘capped bias ratios’?

No. The proposal gives no numerical cap, no units for a resulting budget, and no formula. Any numerical allowance would have to come from an explicitly specified calibration rule and its supporting assumptions, not from the phrase alone.
Would a capped ratio automatically make the exclusion budget conservative?

Not automatically. Its implications depend on how the ratio is defined and whether the cap genuinely covers the departures it is meant to bound. A ratio also requires care if its denominator is small or otherwise poorly determined. The proposal does not establish that the calibrated budgets are conservative in any specified setting.
Is the calibration itself known without error once a negative-control outcome is observed?

No such certainty is stated. If calibration uses observed data, uncertainty in the negative-control information and in the mapping from that information to a budget would matter to the eventual inference claim. Treating a data-derived budget as fixed without justification could leave a gap in a claimed 95% guarantee. The proposal does not specify how calibration uncertainty will be handled.
Does the negative control establish that the exclusion restriction holds?

No. The proposal deliberately works with bounded exclusion violations. A negative-control outcome is proposed as an aid to calibrating how much violation to permit, not as a proof of exact exclusion. It also does not, by itself, establish that a particular budget includes the true departure.
What are the joint 95% multinomial regions for?

They represent uncertainty about the relevant multinomial probabilities jointly at the stated 95% level. Projecting each region through the admissible response-type analysis retains subgroup effect values compatible with probabilities in the region and the calibrated exclusion restrictions. ‘Joint’ is important when the intended inference concerns multiple probabilities together rather than separate statements that may not have a joint guarantee.
Does ‘joint’ automatically mean simultaneous 95% coverage for every subgroup effect?

The joint region can be a basis for simultaneous inference, but the projection and the target coverage event must be defined accordingly. One needs to show that, when the true probabilities lie in the joint region and the maintained restrictions hold, all intended subgroup targets are included as claimed. The proposal does not already establish that projected simultaneous-coverage result.
What role do the response-type LPs play after calibration?

They determine the range of subgroup treatment effects compatible with multinomial probabilities and the applicable subgroup exclusion budgets. Projection would repeat that compatibility calculation over probabilities admitted by the joint region. The resulting population identification endpoints and the confidence sets obtained by projection are related, but they are not the same object.
Can I call the LP endpoints sharp because the proposal calls them sharp response-type LPs?

Sharpness remains a claim to justify for the specified restrictions. The LP must represent all and only the admissible response-type possibilities, and its endpoints must be attainable. If calibration changes the subgroup budgets, any sharpness argument must apply to the bounds under those budgets; merely optimizing a formulated LP is not sufficient proof.
How does using a joint 95% region relate to the broader requirement of uniform coverage with weak instruments?

A joint 95% region may support a coverage argument through projection, but uniform at-least-95% coverage over specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes requires more. The joint-region guarantee, the calibrated-budget assumptions, and the projection argument must all hold throughout the claimed class, including weak-instrument settings. This proposal does not report that those conditions have been verified.
Could a wider calibrated exclusion budget affect the usefulness of the bounds without necessarily changing the joint region’s nominal level?

Yes, conceptually. A more permissive exclusion restriction can admit more response-type possibilities and thus change the subgroup bounds. The 95% label refers to the multinomial region’s stated coverage level; it does not promise narrow projected effect sets. The proposal gives no numerical budget or width comparison from which to infer a particular change.
Does this proposal already establish an improvement over no-instrument Manski bounds?

No. Calibrating budgets and projecting joint regions does not itself show that the sharp subgroup identification bounds improve on the corresponding no-instrument bounds. To answer that part of the broader objective, compare bounds for the same subgroup effect under the calibrated restrictions and a clearly specified no-instrument benchmark.
Should I compare confidence-set widths with Manski identification-bound widths as though they were interchangeable?

No. A confidence set includes uncertainty about the multinomial probabilities; a Manski identification bound concerns population-level compatibility. If the intended claim is about improved identification, compare identification bounds. If it is about confidence-set width, define a comparable no-instrument inferential benchmark. The proposal itself gives neither comparison result.
Does a numerical exclusion budget learned from a negative control remain valid for every subgroup automatically?

No. The proposal specifically calls for subgroup budget calibration, so applying one negative-control relationship uniformly would require justification. Both the relevance of the negative control and the capped-ratio restriction must be appropriate to the subgroup for which a budget is used. No subgroup-specific calibration findings are stated.

Does adopting these limits prove the resulting LP endpoints are sharp?

Would it be accurate to say the decision resolves all uncertainty from negative-control calibration?

Retain calibration using valid negative controls, replace plug-in subgroup exclusion budgets with simultaneous upper confidence limits, and use those limits before projecting the subgroup LP bounds. My hypothesis is that, at first-stage strength 0.03, valid negative controls, a clinical-to-negative-control bias-ratio cap of 1.5, and subgroup size n≥800, simultaneous limits yield at least 95% coverage and at least 1% narrowing relative to no-instrument Manski bounds.

Does n≥800 include a subgroup of exactly 800?
Yes. A subgroup with n=800 meets the size condition. Coverage of exactly 95% and narrowing of exactly 1% would also meet their respective inclusive thresholds.
Is the cap any value up to 1.5?
This hypothesis specifies a cap of 1.5, rather than a range of caps ≤1.5. It makes no prediction here for a different cap, even a smaller one.
And is 1.5 a measured clinical-to-negative-control bias ratio?
No. It is the cap imposed for this hypothesized analysis. The statement does not report a measured bias ratio or give numerical exclusion budgets resulting from calibration.
What does the valid-controls condition contribute?

It is an assumption under which the proposed calibration is to be evaluated. The hypothesis does not establish that any particular negative-control outcome is valid. Validity also does not, by itself, remove uncertainty in the budgets calibrated from those controls; the simultaneous limits are intended to address that separate issue.
Can I infer that simultaneous limits guarantee the 95% result?

No. The ≥95% coverage is an outcome the hypothesis predicts. Its justification would require specifying the limits’ joint confidence property and showing how they enter the projection and support coverage of the defined subgroup target. The word “simultaneous” is not itself a proof of projected-effect coverage.
Does ‘simultaneous’ mean all subgroup limits have to equal one another?

No. It concerns a joint statement about the relevant limits, not equality of their numerical values. The subgroup limits could differ. The hypothesis supplies neither their values nor their construction.
Is the ≥95% figure necessarily a simultaneous coverage claim for every subgroup effect?

The hypothesis says ≥95% coverage but does not define whether the coverage event is simultaneous across subgroup effects or specified separately for each. The simultaneous budget limits should not be mistaken for an automatically established simultaneous effect-coverage guarantee. That coverage event needs to be stated before testing the hypothesis.
What does at least 1% Manski-relative narrowing mean if we compare bound widths?

For the same subgroup effect and a positive-width no-instrument Manski bound, ≥1% narrowing would mean the instrument-based bound is no more than 99% as wide as that benchmark. That explains a possible width criterion; it does not give an observed width or say which endpoint changes.
Does the hypothesis specify whether the 1% refers to identification bounds or projected confidence sets?

It calls for Manski-relative narrowing without explicitly naming which widths are compared. Given the question about bounds, subgroup identification-bound widths are a natural interpretation, but the comparison should be defined before assessment. A gain in identification-bound width and a gain in projected confidence-set width are not interchangeable.
Would a narrower interval necessarily lie entirely within the Manski interval?

No. Smaller width alone does not establish containment. If the intended claim is strict improvement as a set, rather than a relative reduction in width, the interval endpoints must also be compared. The hypothesis provides no endpoint results.
If coverage were at least 95% but narrowing were less than 1%, would the hypothesis hold?

Not in full. It predicts both thresholds under the same stated conditions. Adequate coverage would meet one part, but a gain below 1% would miss the quantitative narrowing part. Conversely, a ≥1% width gain would not compensate for coverage below 95%.
Does n≥800 refer to the number of simulated cohorts?
No. It is a subgroup-size condition. This hypothesis does not specify a number of simulated cohorts or a simulation design.
Can I extend the prediction to subgroups smaller than 800?
No prediction for smaller subgroups is stated. That does not mean they necessarily have inadequate coverage or no Manski-relative gain; it means this particular joint hypothesis is limited to n≥800.
What about first-stage strengths other than 0.03?
They are outside the stated prediction. A result at first-stage strength 0.03 would not by itself establish coverage or narrowing across a weak-instrument grid.
Could a result at n=800 establish the hypothesis for every subgroup with n≥800?

Not automatically. The subgroups and coverage event included in the claim must be defined. Evidence for one evaluated subgroup of size 800 would not alone establish the same outcomes for every subgroup of that size or larger.

Hypothesize that, at first-stage strength 0.03, valid negative controls and a bias-ratio cap of 1.5, together with simultaneous limits on calibrated subgroup exclusion budgets, yield ≥95% coverage and ≥1% Manski-relative narrowing for the specified subgroups with n≥800.
